examples.text: A tittle is more or less the same thing (the dot over an i, for instance), except that it can be traced back to Medieval Latin for a little mark over or under a letter, such as an accent ague or a cedilla. I don't know whether an umlaut is one or two tittles. Maybe it's a jot and a tittle side by side.
examples.ref: 2008, Roy Blount, Alphabet juice: the energies, gists, and spirits of letters:

raw_glosses: (linguistics) An assimilatory process whereby a vowel is pronounced more like a following vocoid that is separated by one or more consonants.
glosses: An assimilatory process whereby a vowel is pronounced more like a following vocoid that is separated by one or more consonants.

raw_glosses: (linguistics) The umlaut process (as above) that occurred historically in Germanic languages whereby back vowels became front vowels when followed by syllable containing a front vocoid (e.g. Germanic lūsiz > Old English lȳs(i) > Modern English lice).
glosses: The umlaut process (as above) that occurred historically in Germanic languages whereby back vowels became front vowels when followed by syllable containing a front vocoid (e.g. Germanic lūsiz > Old English lȳs(i) > Modern English lice).

raw_glosses: (orthography) The diacritical mark ( ¨ ) placed over a vowel when it indicates a (rounded) front vowel
glosses: The diacritical mark ( ¨ ) placed over a vowel when it indicates a (rounded) front vowel

examples.text: "Naïve" takes an umlaut because it is pronounced as two syllables.

California, like several other states, prohibits the use of diacritical marks or accents on official documents. That means no tilde (~), no accent grave (`), no umlaut (¨) and certainly no cedilla (¸).
